newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: OSCE envoy sees Albania troops within two weeks.
newsitem.headline: OSCE envoy sees Albania troops within two weeks.

text.p: An Italian-led force to guard aid deliveries to crisis-torn Albania could be dispatched within two weeks, the Albania envoy of Europe's top security body the OSCE, Franz Vranitzky, said on Saturday.
The U.N. Security Council late on Friday authorized the mission to help the country recover from violence and anarchy.

The vote "creates the diplomatic and politcal basis" for the Organisation for Security and Cooperation Europe's (OSCE) active involvement in Albania, former Austrian chancellor Vranitzky told the Austrian news agency APA in an interview.
Vranitzky said the U.N. Security Council's vote was "very positive".
"We don't have any time to lose in Albania," he added.

Vranitzky said he would get in touch immediately with those nations that had promised to contribute troops to the mission to coordinate the next steps. "I hope the mission can start in one to two weeks," he said.
The OSCE envoy said he planned to travel to Tirana in the "very near future", possibly as early as next week, to coordinate the mission with the Albanian government.
He said the mission's main goal was to support the Tirana government of President Sali Berisha in restoring calm and order in the Balkan nation.

Greece, France, Spain, and Portugal have said they are prepared to commit troops to Albania. Turkey and Romania have also expressed willingness to take part. Neutral Austria said it would need a U.N. mandate, while the United States, Britain and Germany said they would not participate.

Some 2,500 soldiers are expected to take part, with the same number of soldiers in reserve should they be needed. The mandate of the force runs for three months at which time the U.N. council can decide whether it should be extended.
Albania has been swept by violence since a string of dubious pyramid investment schemes collapsed in January, wiping out the life savings of many impoverished Albanians.

Rebels seized the country's south in March. Since then, gangs have roamed the area, stealing, looting, killing and creating a food crisis, prompting the government to aks for foreign military assistance.
